result:
Medieval scribes complained in the margins, and this is one of my favorite facts about the history of writing. Copying a manuscript meant months hunched over vellum in an unheated room, and the scribes sometimes left small notes at the edges of the page, addressed to no one. "The ink is thin." "Oh, my hand." "Thank God, it will soon be dark." One wrote, "Writing is excessive drudgery. It crooks your back, it dims your sight, it twists your stomach and your sides." Another, finishing a long book, added: "Now I've written the whole thing; for Christ's sake give me a drink."

I like these notes because they break the frame. The main text is usually solemn: scripture, commentary, law. It was meant to last, and it speaks in the voice of an institution. Then two inches to the left, a man is cold and wants his dinner. The page holds both, and the complaint has aged better than some of the theology.

A ninth-century Irish monk wrote a poem about his cat, Pangur Bán, comparing the cat's mouse-hunting to his own hunt for meaning in difficult texts. Each of them, he says, is happy at his own work, and neither gets in the other's way. The poem survives in a notebook otherwise full of Latin hymns and grammar notes.

The scribes probably never expected anyone to read these lines. They wrote them for the relief of writing them. A thousand years later, they're the part of the page I'd read first, ahead of whatever the scribe was actually told to copy.
